claims_disputed.claim: The pipeline detects requirement faults (97.3% of 256 mutations; 63/64 end-to-end injected defects).
claims_disputed.reason: In both experiments, 'detected' means the mutant's encoding is not SMT-equivalent to the known-correct original encoding (Table 1b; §2.6 condition b). That is change detection. It flags any semantic edit, intended or not, and it needs the correct version to exist already. The one reference-free check, global consistency, caught 0 of 64 injected defects, because every mutated set stayed satisfiable (§2.6). Nothing shows the pipeline finding faults in a specification that has no trusted reference.

pattern_stance_changes.reason: The comparison is not split. Model, prompt, verifier gate and five-repair budget are held fixed, and the counterexample condition beats requirement-only, generic and no-feedback repair on final accuracy (98.5 vs 80.0, 58.5, 55.4) and on repair success (97.1 vs 59.4, 10.0, 12.1), Fig. 4. The verifier also being the grader limits what 'accuracy' means. That limit is already reflected in the moderate grade on the claim; it does not make the result mixed.

No arm compares the formal pipeline with a non-formal alternative. Candidates would be an LLM ambiguity check, the existing Event-B, Circus or ASM formalizations of this case study, or test-based checking. All four CEGR conditions use the same SMT gate, so that comparison belongs to P16. The audits, round-trip and ambiguity loop have no comparator, and nothing in the paper shows formal methods losing or splitting.

missed_issues: §2.7 and Table 5 are internally inconsistent. Table 5 gives r3 14 distinct encodings 'before' from N=5 samples, which is impossible. The reported 44.0% pairwise agreement also conflicts with 52 of 64 requirements having a single encoding: those alone give at least 520 of 640 agreeing pairs, or 81%.

The CEGR repair suffix (App. D) includes 'Conflicts with your previous answer: <conflict_lines>', which names the answer fields that are wrong. Because the action fields are Boolean, the full-CEGR condition comes close to handing the model the verifier's answer. The 18.5-point gap over requirement-only feedback therefore measures answer leakage as much as fault localization.

The requirement-only repair success rate (59.4%) does not follow from that condition's own first-attempt and final accuracies. Going from 46.2% to 80.0% of 65 questions means 22 of 35 rejected answers were fixed, which is 62.9%. The other three conditions reconcile exactly.

Gold answers exist for the 65 questions (Table 6), but scoring uses only verifier acceptance. The paper never reports how often verifier-safe answers match the gold answers, so an error in the LLM-generated model would go unnoticed.

On the original specification the reference-free audits found no defect: the spec is consistent, 39/39 conditionals are non-vacuous and 64/64 requirements are violatable. The authors themselves call the two redundancies review signals, not defects (Table 1a, §2.4). The audits' defect yield on real requirements is therefore not shown.

Each of the 12 clarified rewrites in Table 5 resolves the ambiguity by choosing a reading, not only r3. For example, r23 and r24 assign the 200 mL/min endpoint to the lower band, and r56 and r57 import numeric limits from r42 and r44. These are owner decisions made by the model without any stakeholder input.

§2.6 says the Exp 3 mutants were written manually, but App. D says they were LLM-translated. Its fault-type mix (34 limit, 24 mode, 2 false-alarm, 4 value) does not match the balanced four categories of Exp 1. Table 4 also lists 6 repairs and 'default' temperature, against the 5 retries and temperature 0 stated in §2.3.
P17 (static analysis or checker feedback in the loop) describes the SMT solver feedback better than P16 (execution-based tests or compile), and the review did not tag it.
note: I agree with admit_with_caveats, COI none and the review's central reading: every success metric is self-referential, and the four-way feedback comparison is the one isolating result. My scores differ on reproducibility (2 vs 1, since the case study is public and most prompts are printed) and relevance (2 vs 3, since SMT over linear arithmetic fits device limits far better than service or ingestion specs). I lower the fault-detection claim to unsupported, because detection means differing from an already-known correct encoding, and the reference-free consistency audit caught none of the 64 injected defects. I move P16 to supports because the feedback comparison is not split, and P35 to introduces because no arm tests formal methods against a non-formal alternative. Treat the §2.7 agreement numbers as unreliable: Table 5 reports 14 encodings from 5 samples.
